title: CSC3710 2026-09-17: Regular Sets and Regular Expressions

questions.q: In the recursive definition of the regular sets over an alphabet Σ, which of these is NOT a basis set?
questions.explain: The basis is ∅, {λ}, and {a} for each a ∈ Σ. Σ* is regular, but you get it from the basis using union and Kleene star. It is not a basis set itself.

questions.q: Which operations make up the recursive step in the definition of regular sets?
questions.explain: If X and Y are regular, then X ∪ Y, XY, and X* are regular. Intersection and complement are not part of the definition.

questions.q: The closure clause says a set is regular over Σ only if it can be obtained from the basis sets by a finite number of applications of the recursive step.
questions.explain: Closure means nothing else is regular. Every regular set has to be built from the basis in finitely many steps.

questions.q: Applying a recursive-step operation to a regular set always gives a new set, different from the one you started with.
questions.explain: Not always. For example {λ}* = {λ}, so starring {λ} just gives {λ} back.

questions.q: You are proving that the set of strings over {a, b} that end with aaa is regular. You already have {aaa} and {a, b}* as regular sets. Which final step finishes the proof?
questions.explain: Every string of {a, b}* gets aaa added at the end: λ·aaa = aaa, a·aaa = aaaa, b·aaa = baaa, and so on. Order matters. {aaa}{a, b}* is the set of strings that START with aaa.

questions.q: In a step-by-step proof, {a} and {b} are already known to be regular. Which part of the definition justifies that {a, b} is regular?
questions.explain: {a} ∪ {b} = {a, b}, so it is regular by union. {a, b} is not a basis set, because basis sets contain a single alphabet symbol.

questions.q: A student's proof contains the line '{ab} is regular by basis.' What is wrong with it?
choices: {ab} is not a basis set. It is regular because it is the concatenation {a}{b} of two basis sets.
{ab} is regular only by Kleene star, as {ab} = {a, b}*.
questions.explain: The basis sets are ∅, {λ}, and single-symbol sets {a}. The set {ab} contains a two-symbol string, so you justify it with concatenation: {a}{b} = {ab}.

questions.q: The set {aaa}{a, b}* is the set of strings over {a, b} that end with aaa.
questions.explain: Concatenation order matters. {aaa}{a, b}* puts aaa first, so it is the strings that start with aaa. The strings that end with aaa are {a, b}*{aaa}.

questions.q: What is the shortest string in the set of strings over {a, b} that end with aaa?
questions.explain: {a, b}*{aaa} contains λ·aaa = aaa. λ itself is not in the set.

questions.q: In regular expressions, what is the precedence of the operators, from most binding to least binding?
choices: Kleene star, then concatenation, then union
Concatenation, then Kleene star, then union
Union, then concatenation, then Kleene star
Kleene star, then union, then concatenation
questions.explain: Star binds tightest, then concatenation, then union. That is why ab* means a(b*) and ab ∪ c means (ab) ∪ c.

questions.q: What does the regular expression ab* mean?
choices: a(b*): an a followed by zero or more b's
(ab)*: zero or more copies of ab
a(b+): an a followed by one or more b's
questions.explain: Star binds tighter than concatenation, so it applies only to b. To repeat ab you need (ab)*.

questions.q: How is ab ∪ aba* parsed?
questions.explain: Star first, so it applies only to the last a. Then concatenation, then union. The expression is {ab} ∪ {ab, aba, abaa, ...}.

questions.q: What does ab ∪ c mean?
questions.explain: Concatenation binds tighter than union, so the expression describes {ab, c}.

questions.q: What does the shorthand u+ abbreviate?
questions.explain: u+ = uu*, which means one or more copies of u. It works the same way as X+ = XX* for sets.

questions.q: Which is a shorter way to write (a ∪ b)(a ∪ b)*?
questions.explain: uu* = u+, so (a ∪ b)(a ∪ b)* = (a ∪ b)+, the nonempty strings over {a, b}. a+ ∪ b+ is wrong because it leaves out mixed strings like ab.

questions.q: How many strings are in the set described by (a ∪ b)³?
questions.explain: (a ∪ b)³ = (a ∪ b)(a ∪ b)(a ∪ b). There are 2 choices for each of 3 positions, so 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 strings.

questions.q: ab*b and (ab)*b describe the same set.
questions.explain: Adding parentheses changes the expression. b belongs to the set described by (ab)*b (zero copies of ab), but every string described by ab*b starts with a.

questions.q: Which regular set is described by the regular expression (ab*b)*?
questions.explain: Drop the curly braces to go from sets to expressions. Each symbol becomes a single-symbol set, and the operators stay in the same places.

questions.q: Which statement uses the right terminology for how a regular expression relates to a set of strings?
choices: The regular expression a*b describes the set {b, ab, aab, ...}.
The regular expression a*b is equal to the set {b, ab, aab, ...}.
The set {b, ab, aab, ...} describes the regular expression a*b.
The regular expression a*b is a subset of {a, b}*.
questions.explain: An expression and a set are different kinds of objects, so the expression describes the set. For membership, say that a string belongs to the set described by the expression.

questions.q: Which strings belong to the set described by a*b?
questions.explain: a*b is zero or more a's followed by exactly one b. abb has two b's and bab has an a after a b. λ has no b.

questions.q: Over {a, b}, 'strings that end with b' is an accurate description of the set described by a*b.
questions.explain: Too loose. bab and abb end with b but are not in a*b. 'Ends with b' is (a ∪ b)*b. The precise description of a*b is zero or more a's followed by a single b.

questions.q: Which expression is equivalent to ab*b?
questions.explain: b*b gives λ·b = b, b·b = bb, and so on, which is one or more b's. So ab*b is an a followed by one or more b's: ab+.

questions.q: Which strings belong to the set described by (ab*b)*?
questions.explain: The building block is ab*b = {ab, abb, abbb, ...}, and the star allows any number of blocks, including zero (λ). abbab = (abb)(ab) and abab = (ab)(ab). In aab and abba some a is not followed by a b, and ba does not start with a.

questions.q: How many strings of length exactly 4 are in the set described by (ab*b)*?
questions.explain: The blocks are ab (length 2), abb (3), abbb (4), and so on. To get length 4 you can use ab·ab = abab or the single block abbb. That is 2 strings.

questions.q: Which is the best plain-language description of the set described by (ab*b)*?
choices: λ, or a string that starts with a in which every a is immediately followed by at least one b
Strings that start with a and end with b
Zero or more a's followed by one or more b's
Any string of a's and b's that ends in b
questions.explain: The string has to be a sequence of ab...b blocks, possibly zero of them. 'Starts with a and ends with b' would let in aab and leave out λ. 'Zero or more a's then one or more b's' describes a*b+.

questions.q: The string aabbbbbbaabb belongs to the set described by a(a ∪ bb)*.
questions.explain: Split it as a · (a)(bb)(bb)(bb)(a)(a)(bb). There is a leading a, and after that every piece is an a block or a bb block.

questions.q: Which strings belong to the set described by a(a ∪ bb)*?
questions.explain: After the leading a, b's can only appear in pairs. a = a·λ, abb = a·(bb), abba = a·(bb)(a). abab and abbba each have a single b. bb has no leading a.

questions.q: What is the shortest string in the set described by a(a ∪ bb)*?
questions.explain: Take zero blocks from the starred part: a·λ = a.

questions.q: Which description matches the set described by (a ∪ b)(a ∪ b)*bbb?
choices: Strings that end in bbb and have length at least 4
Strings of length at least 4 that start with a
questions.explain: One required symbol, then anything (including λ), then bbb. This is (a ∪ b)+bbb, so the length is at least 4 and the string ends in bbb.

questions.q: The string bbb belongs to the set described by (a ∪ b)(a ∪ b)*bbb.
questions.explain: The leading (a ∪ b) requires one symbol before the final bbb, so the shortest strings have length 4 (abbb, bbbb).

questions.q: How many strings of length exactly 4 are in the set described by (a ∪ b)(a ∪ b)*bbb?
questions.explain: With length 4 the starred part must be λ, so the string is (a or b) followed by bbb: abbb and bbbb.

questions.q: Which string does NOT belong to the set described by (aba)*?
questions.explain: (aba)* is λ or copies of aba placed back to back. abab is not a whole number of aba blocks.

questions.q: ab ∪ aba* is equivalent to aba*.
questions.explain: aba* = {ab, aba, abaa, ...} already contains ab (zero a's). Sets don't count duplicates, so the 'ab ∪' part is redundant.

questions.q: (a ∪ bb ∪ aa)* is equivalent to (a ∪ bb)*.
questions.explain: The aa block is redundant. Anything built with an aa block can be built with two a blocks instead.

questions.q: Which string proves that (a ∪ bb)* and (a ∪ b)* are NOT equivalent?
questions.explain: b belongs to the set described by (a ∪ b)*, but (a ∪ bb)* only produces b's in pairs. λ, aa, and bb are in both sets.

questions.q: What is enough to prove that two regular expressions are NOT equivalent?
choices: One string that belongs to the set described by one expression but not to the set described by the other
Showing the two expressions are written with different symbols
Showing one set has more elements than the other
Listing the first ten strings of each set
questions.explain: A single counterexample is a complete proof. Expressions that look different can still be equivalent, e.g. ab ∪ aba* and aba*. Matching the first ten strings doesn't settle anything either way.

questions.q: When two regular expressions describe infinite sets, arguing that 'one set has more elements than the other' is a sound way to show they differ.
questions.explain: Infinite sets behave strangely. For example, the natural numbers and the rational numbers have the same cardinality. Name a specific string that is in one set and not the other instead.

questions.q: Which expression is equivalent to a ∪ a*?
questions.explain: a is already in a*, so the union adds nothing. Note that a+ and aa* are wrong because they leave out λ, which a* contains.

questions.q: Which expression is equivalent to (a ∪ aa)*?
questions.explain: The aa block is redundant because aa is two a blocks. With a alone you can make λ, a, aa, aaa, ..., which is a*. (aa)* would leave out the odd lengths.

questions.q: Are a*b* and (ab)* equivalent?
choices: Yes, they describe the same set
No: a belongs to the set described by a*b* but not to the set described by (ab)*
No: ab belongs to the set described by (ab)* but not to the set described by a*b*
No: λ belongs to one set but not the other
questions.explain: a = a·λ is in a*b*, but every nonempty string in (ab)* has even length. ab and λ are in both sets. abab would also work as a counterexample in the other direction.

questions.q: Any regular expression that contains a Kleene star describes an infinite set.
questions.explain: Counterexamples: λ* = λ, ∅* = λ, and aaλ* describes the finite set {aa}.

questions.q: A regular expression with no Kleene star (and no +) describes a finite set.
questions.explain: Union and concatenation of finite sets stay finite, and a regular expression can't use '...' to list infinitely many strings. You need a star somewhere to get an infinite set.

questions.q: What set does λ* describe?
questions.explain: Any number of copies of λ concatenated together is still λ, so {λ}* = {λ}.

questions.q: What set does ∅* describe?
questions.explain: The star always includes zero copies, which gives λ. There are no strings in ∅ to make anything longer, so ∅* = {λ}.

questions.q: What set does aaλ* describe?
questions.explain: λ* describes {λ}, and aa·λ = aa. The set is {aa}, so it is finite even though the expression has a star.

questions.q: Does (λ ∪ ∅)*ab describe a finite or an infinite set?
choices: Infinite, because it contains a Kleene star
questions.explain: λ ∪ ∅ describes {λ}, and {λ}* = {λ}. Concatenating with ab gives {ab}. λab and λλab are the same string as ab.

questions.q: What set does ∅a* describe?
questions.explain: Concatenation with ∅ always gives ∅, because there is no string in ∅ to put in front. So the star doesn't make this set infinite.

questions.q: Which regular expressions describe the strings over {a, b, c} of length exactly 3?
choices: (a ∪ b ∪ c)(a ∪ b ∪ c)(a ∪ b ∪ c)
aaa ∪ aab ∪ aac ∪ ... ∪ ccc (all 27 strings listed with union)
questions.explain: Listing all 27 strings is fine because the set is finite, and so is choosing one of a, b, c three times. (abc)³ is the single string abcabcabc. a³ ∪ b³ ∪ c³ is only {aaa, bbb, ccc}.

questions.q: How many strings over {a, b, c} have length exactly 3?
questions.explain: There are 3 choices for each of 3 positions: 3 × 3 × 3 = 27.

questions.q: Which regular expressions describe the strings over {a, b, c} of length less than 3?
choices: λ ∪ a ∪ b ∪ c ∪ (a ∪ b ∪ c)(a ∪ b ∪ c)
(a ∪ b ∪ c ∪ λ)(a ∪ b ∪ c ∪ λ)
a ∪ b ∪ c ∪ (a ∪ b ∪ c)(a ∪ b ∪ c)
questions.explain: Length less than 3 means lengths 0, 1, and 2. The second form works because each factor can contribute λ or one symbol. The third leaves out λ, and (a ∪ b ∪ c)* allows any length.

questions.q: Which regular expression describes the strings over {a, b, c} of length greater than 3?
choices: (a ∪ b ∪ c)(a ∪ b ∪ c)(a ∪ b ∪ c)(a ∪ b ∪ c)(a ∪ b ∪ c)*
(a ∪ b ∪ c)(a ∪ b ∪ c)(a ∪ b ∪ c)(a ∪ b ∪ c)*
(a ∪ b ∪ c)(a ∪ b ∪ c)(a ∪ b ∪ c)(a ∪ b ∪ c)
questions.explain: Greater than 3 means 4 or more: four required symbols, then nothing or anything. The second gives length 3 or more. The third gives exactly 4. The fourth gives multiples of 4, including λ.

questions.q: Which regular expression describes the strings over {a, b, c} of length at least 2?
choices: (a ∪ b ∪ c)(a ∪ b ∪ c)(a ∪ b ∪ c)*
questions.explain: Two required symbols, then anything. The second gives length at least 1, the third gives exactly 2, and the fourth is just (a ∪ b ∪ c)*.

questions.q: Which regular expression describes the strings over {a, b} that end with ab?
questions.explain: Anything (including λ), then ab at the end. The shortest strings are ab, aab, bab. ab(a ∪ b)* is 'starts with ab', and (a ∪ b)*ab(a ∪ b)* is 'contains ab'. a*b*ab leaves out strings like abaab.

questions.q: Why is (a ∪ b)*aa(a ∪ b)*bb(a ∪ b)* NOT a correct expression for 'strings over {a, b} that contain both aa and bb as substrings'?
choices: It forces aa to come before bb, so it leaves out strings like bbaa
It includes strings that contain no aa at all
questions.explain: Every string it describes has an aa somewhere before a bb. To fix it, union in the other order: ... ∪ (a ∪ b)*bb(a ∪ b)*aa(a ∪ b)*.

questions.q: Someone proposes (a ∪ b)*(aa ∪ bb)(a ∪ b)*(aa ∪ bb)(a ∪ b)* for 'strings over {a, b} that contain both aa and bb'. Which string is a counterexample showing it is wrong?
questions.explain: Each (aa ∪ bb) chooses independently, so you can choose bb both times. bbbb = bb·λ·bb belongs to the proposed set but contains no aa. The other three strings contain both aa and bb, so they belong to both sets.

questions.q: Which expressions describe the strings over {a, b} of length two or more in which all a's precede all b's? Count strings made only of a's (like aa) or only of b's (like bbb) as members.
questions.explain: The set is every a...ab...b string of length at least 2. a+b+ requires both letters, so it leaves out aa and bb. a*b* includes λ, a, and b, which are too short. (a ∪ b)(a ∪ b)(a ∪ b)* lets in ba. The middle part of a*(aa ∪ ab ∪ bb)b* guarantees length at least 2 and keeps the a's first.

questions.q: For a given set there is exactly one correct regular expression, and any other correct-looking form has to be simplified into it.
questions.explain: Many different regular expressions describe the same set, and all of them are correct. For example, the 27-string union and (a ∪ b ∪ c)³ both describe the strings of length 3 over {a, b, c}.
